is drawn by continuous motion along the entire length *Aa*; and the trapezoid described by that motion, or the rectangle *Aa* x $\frac{1}{2}$ *a B* equal to it, will be equal to the sum of all *MN* x *CM*, and therefore to the sum of all *Dd* x *DK*, that is, to the area *BKVT a*. Q. E. D.

*Corol.* Hence, from the law of resistance and the difference of the arcs *Ca*, *CB* and *Aa*, the proportion of resistance to gravity can be deduced very closely.

For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*; and thus the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to $\frac{1}{2} Aa$. Therefore, since *DK* is the exponent of the resistance, and the length of the pendulum is the exponent of gravity, the resistance to gravity will be as $\frac{1}{2} Aa$ to the length of the pendulum; exactly as demonstrated in prop. xxviii.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be an ellipse very closely. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, were to describe the length *BA* in one complete oscillation, the velocity at any point *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* applied to the diameter *AB* of the circle. Therefore, since *Ba* in a resisting medium and *BA* in a non-resisting medium are described in approximately equal times; and therefore the velocities at individual points of *Ba* are very nearly as the velocities at the corresponding points of the length *BA*, as *Ba* is to *BA*; the velocity at point *D* in a resisting medium will be as the ordinate applied to the circle or ellipse described upon the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be an ellipse very closely. Since the resistance is supposed to be proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the midpoint *O*; and the ellipse *BRVSa*, with center *O* and semi-axes *OB*, *OV*, will equal the figure *BKVT a*, and the rectangle *Aa* x *BO* equal to it, very closely. Therefore *Aa* x *BO* is to *OV* x *BO* as the area of this ellipse is to *OV* x *BO*: that is, *Aa* to *OV* as the area of a semicircle is to the square of the radius, or as 11 to 7 approximately: And therefore $\frac{7}{11} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the squared ratio of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be nearly a parabola having *V* as its vertex and *OV* as its axis, and therefore will be equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV* very closely. Therefore, the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV*, and therefore *OV* is equal to $\frac{3}{4} Aa$: and therefore the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as $\frac{3}{4} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum.

<summary>Newton calculates the relationship between the resistance and gravity of a pendulum by analyzing the area of the figures formed by velocity and resistance over time, specifically under linear and squared resistance models.</summary>
